sections.title: Red cap and shape
sections.text: The cap is about 3–10 cm across. It is typically vivid to cherry red, but may fade toward pink or whitish with age or weather. It starts convex, spreads out, and becomes slightly depressed in the centre. The smooth surface is viscid when wet; the cap skin separates readily, often over much of the radius. These features vary and cannot identify the species on their own.

sections.title: Gills, stem and flesh
sections.text: The white to pale cream gills are crowded, fairly broad, attached to the stem, and fragile. The brittle white stem is usually 4–10 cm long and may widen slightly toward the base. There is no ring or volva. The flesh is white; it may show a pink tint immediately beneath the cap cuticle, without the whole flesh being pink. The spore print is white. A faintly fruity odour is sometimes reported.

sections.title: Habitat and season
sections.text: Russula emetica is ectomycorrhizal, associated mainly with conifers, especially pines. It grows on the ground among mosses, sometimes in sphagnum or peaty places, as well as in mixed woods. It fruits in summer and autumn, often from July to October depending on climate. Reported habitats and species boundaries vary with region and taxonomic concept.

sections.title: Toxicity and cautious identification
sections.text: This brittlegill is poisonous and may cause digestive upset, including nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps and diarrhoea. Red-capped russulas look very similar; identification to species cannot rely on cap colour alone and may require several characters or microscopy. Do not eat a specimen identified from a photo or illustration. After a suspected ingestion, contact a poison centre or medical service promptly.

traits: Vivid to cherry-red cap, smooth and viscid when wet, 3–10 cm across; convex then spreading and sometimes depressed
Cap skin usually separates readily; colour may fade toward pink or white
White to pale cream gills, crowded, fairly broad and attached to the stem
White brittle stem, often slightly wider toward the base; no ring or volva
White flesh, sometimes pink only immediately beneath the cap cuticle; white spore print
Mycorrhizal mainly with conifers; among mosses and sometimes sphagnum; summer and autumn
Poisonous: may cause digestive upset; red russulas are difficult to distinguish
safetyNote: Poisonous: Russula emetica may cause nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps and diarrhoea. Red-capped russulas look alike, and a photo or cap colour cannot provide a safe identification. Do not eat an uncertain specimen. After a suspected ingestion, promptly contact a poison centre or medical service.
